stem: A security team wants developers to find SQL injection and buffer overflow flaws in source code automatically on every commit, before the application is deployed to any environment. Which technique BEST fits?
options: Static analysis integrated into the CI pipeline
Dynamic scanning of the staging environment
An annual external penetration test
Fuzz testing against production endpoints
explanations: Static application security testing analyzes source code without executing it, so it can run on every commit in CI and flag injection and overflow patterns before any deployment.
Dynamic testing requires a running application in a deployed environment, so it cannot satisfy the before-deployment, per-commit requirement.
An annual penetration test is far too infrequent for per-commit feedback and examines a built, deployed system rather than source.
Fuzzing production is the latest possible point of discovery and risks disrupting live service; the goal is to catch flaws before deployment.

stem: To minimize the cost of fixing security defects, at which point in the software development life cycle should security requirements FIRST be defined?
options: During the requirements phase
During implementation, as code is written
During system testing before release
After deployment, through patching
explanations: Security requirements defined alongside functional requirements shape the design from the start, where changes cost the least.
Waiting until coding leaves design-level flaws baked in; developers can only secure what the design allows.
Defects found in testing require rework of already-built software at many times the early-phase cost.
Post-deployment patching is the most expensive and riskiest point to introduce security.

stem: A code review finds user input concatenated directly into SQL statements. Which change MOST effectively eliminates the injection risk?
options: Escaping quote characters in user input
Suppressing database error messages to users
Using parameterized queries for all database access
Limiting the length of every input field
explanations: Escaping is a fragile filter — encoding tricks and second-order injection routinely bypass it.
Hiding errors reduces information leakage but leaves the injection fully exploitable blind.
Parameterized queries separate code from data, so user input can never be interpreted as SQL — the flaw class is eliminated rather than filtered.
Length limits constrain payload size, and short injection payloads still work.

stem: A hospital is buying a commercial off-the-shelf clinical application and cannot review its source code. Which approach gives the BEST assurance of the product's security before purchase?
options: A contract clause promising secure coding practices
Independent security certifications and test evidence for the product
An antivirus scan of the installation media
Waiting for other hospitals to report problems
explanations: A promise in a contract allocates liability but provides no evidence the software is actually secure.
Third-party evaluations, penetration test attestations, and certifications give evidence-based assurance without needing source access.
Scanning the installer checks for known malware, not for design or implementation weaknesses in the product.
Relying on others' incidents is reactive and offers no assurance before purchase.

stem: A development organization tracks the percentage of code exercised by its security test suite, yet critical vulnerabilities keep shipping from areas the metric rates highly. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The coverage tool is miscounting executed lines
All the vulnerabilities are in third-party libraries
Developers are skipping the test suite before release
Coverage shows code was executed, not that security outcomes were asserted
explanations: Tool error is possible but would not systematically produce shipping vulnerabilities in well-covered areas release after release.
Some flaws may be inherited, but the metric rates the organization's own code highly and those areas keep shipping flaws too.
If the suite were skipped, the coverage figures themselves would collapse rather than stay high.
Executing a line is not testing it: without assertions about security behavior — authorization, validation, error paths — covered code can remain completely unverified.
